procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the learned Magistrate directing payment of maintenance at the rate of Rs. 25 per month to the appellant No. 2 and refusing the claim of the appellant No. 1 for maintenance.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellants filed a revision petition (Criminal R.P. No.) against the order of the Magistrate. The respondent also filed another petition being Criminal R.P. No. 188 of 1979 against the order of the learned Magistrate. The High Court dismissed the Criminal Revision Petition of the appellants and allowed that of the respondent.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants preferred two appeals by special leave (Criminal Appeal Nos. 462A-463 of 1981) against the judgment of the High Court.

decision.appeal_result: Criminal Appeal No. 462A of 1981 is allowed and Criminal Appeal No. 463 of 1981 is dismissed.
directions: The order of the High Court is set aside in so far as it disallows the claim of the appellant No. 2, Sulekha, for maintenance as granted by the learned Magistrate.
The Criminal Revision Petition No.188 of 1979 is dismissed.
Criminal Appeal No. 462A of 1981 is allowed.
Criminal Appeal No. 463 of 1981 is dismissed.
There will be no order for costs in either of the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its criminal revisional jurisdiction under Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, is justified in re-assessing evidence and substituting its own finding on a question of fact for that of the trial court.

facts: A trial Magistrate found that appellant No. 2 was the illegitimate child of the respondent and granted her maintenance.
In a revision petition, the High Court conducted a "re-assessment of the evidence" and came to the opposite conclusion, finding that the appellant was not the illegitimate child of the respondent.
As a result, the High Court set aside the Magistrate's order for maintenance.
law: The scope of the High Court's criminal revisional jurisdiction under Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is limited.
Re-appreciation of evidence and substituting the High Court's own view on a question of fact is impermissible under this jurisdiction.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had improperly engaged in a "re-assessment of the evidence" concerning the paternity of the child.
By doing so, the High Court substituted its own view for that of the trial Magistrate on a question of fact, which exceeded the scope of its revisional powers.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was not justified in re-assessing the evidence and substituting its own finding for that of the trial court, as this is impermissible within the High Court's criminal revisional jurisdiction under Section 401.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant No. 2 was the illegitimate child of the respondent and entitled to maintenance.

facts: The Magistrate, after appreciating the evidence, found that while appellant No. 1 was not the respondent's wife, appellant No. 2 was his illegitimate child and was entitled to maintenance.
The High Court, in its revisional jurisdiction, re-assessed the evidence and came to the opposite conclusion, finding that appellant No. 2 was not the child of the respondent.
law: The question of whether a person is the legitimate or illegitimate child of another is a "pre-eminently question of fact."
A High Court, exercising its revisional jurisdiction, is not justified in substituting its own view for that of the trial court on a question of fact.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court committed an error by re-assessing the evidence and overturning the Magistrate's finding of fact.
The Supreme Court noted that the Magistrate had taken great pains to analyze the evidence before reaching his conclusion.
After considering the evidence on record for itself, the Supreme Court agreed with the Magistrate's finding that appellant No. 2 was the illegitimate child of the respondent.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the High Court was wrong to interfere with the Magistrate's factual finding. It set aside the High Court's order and restored the Magistrate's decision, thereby confirming that appellant No. 2 was the respondent's illegitimate child and entitled to maintenance.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellant No. 1 was the married wife of the respondent.

facts: The Magistrate, after considering the evidence presented by the parties, came to the factual finding that the alleged marriage between appellant No. 1 and the respondent was not proven.
The High Court, in its judgment, upheld the Magistrate's finding that appellant No. 1 was not the wife of the respondent.
law: The question of whether a person is the married wife of another is a "pre-eminently question of fact."
A court in its revisional jurisdiction is not justified in substituting its own view for that of the trial court on a question of fact.
application: The Supreme Court noted that both the Magistrate and the High Court had reached the same conclusion on the factual issue of the marriage.
The Supreme Court's reasoning in the case was that the High Court should not have re-assessed the evidence on a question of fact determined by the Magistrate.
Since the lower courts had already made a concurrent finding of fact that the marriage was not proven, the Supreme Court did not disturb this finding.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the concurrent findings of the Magistrate and the High Court, which determined as a matter of fact that the marriage of appellant No. 1 to the respondent was not proven. Therefore, her claim to be the respondent's wife was rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its criminal revisional jurisdiction under Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, is justified in re-assessing evidence and substituting its own finding on a question of fact for that of the trial court.
appellant_arguments: The appellants' appeal implies they argued that the High Court was not justified in re-assessing the evidence and overturning the Magistrate's factual finding regarding the paternity of appellant No. 2.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's revision petition to the High Court (which was allowed) implies they argued that the High Court was justified in re-assessing the evidence to correct the Magistrate's finding of fact.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant No. 2 was the illegitimate child of the respondent and entitled to maintenance.
appellant_arguments: Appellant No. 2 is the illegitimate child of the respondent and is therefore entitled to maintenance under Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
respondent_arguments: Appellant No. 2 was not his child, either legitimate or illegitimate.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellant No. 1 was the married wife of the respondent.
appellant_arguments: Appellant No. 1 was the legally married wife of the respondent.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court, exercising its criminal revisional jurisdiction, is not justified in re-assessing evidence to substitute its own view for that of a lower court on a question of fact.
obiter: The determination of whether a person is the married wife of another, or whether a child is the legitimate or illegitimate child of another, are pre-eminently questions of fact.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court, in its criminal revisional jurisdiction under Section 401 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, is not justified in making a re-assessment of the evidence and substituting its own finding for that of the trial court on what are pre-eminently questions of fact, such as the determination of marriage and paternity. The High Court committed an error in re-assessing the evidence to overturn the Magistrate's finding that appellant No. 2 was the illegitimate child of the respondent.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a particular issue, such as the status of a marriage or the paternity of a child, constitutes a 'question of fact' which is generally outside the scope of re-assessment in criminal revisional jurisdiction.
why_appellant_lost: Regarding the claim of appellant No. 1 to be the married wife of the respondent, the Supreme Court affirmed the concurrent findings of the lower courts. The text states: 'The learned Magistrate by his order dated March 24, 1979 came to the finding that the marriage of the respondent with the appellant No. 1, as alleged, was not proved and, as such, the appellant No. 1 was not the wife of the respondent.' This finding was upheld by the High Court and her subsequent appeal was dismissed.
why_respondent_won: The respondent successfully defended against the claim that appellant No. 1 was his wife because the trial court, after considering the evidence, found that the marriage was not proved. The text notes: 'The learned Maglstrate after considering the evidence, as adduced by the parties, held that the appellant No. l was not the wife of the respondent.' This factual finding was sustained through the appellate process.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning reinforces the judicial policy of deferring to the trial court on findings of fact, as the trial judge is best positioned to analyze the evidence. This is evident in the court's statement: 'We have ourselves considered the evidence on record and we agree with the learned Magistrate, who had taken DllCh pains in analysing the evidence, that the appellant No.2 was the illegitimate child of the respondent.'
